Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters View image in fullscreen Chuck Edwards attends a hearing on on Capitol Hill in April. Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters House of Representatives US House ethics panel recommends censure for Republican Chuck Edwards North Carolina congressman’s campaign rejects committee finding that Edwards ‘engaged in sexual harassment’ Chris Stein in Washington Mon 3 Aug 2026 18.52 EDT First published on Mon 3 Aug 2026 17.06 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The US House of Representatives ethics committee on Monday recommended that Chuck Edwards, a Republican congressman, face censure after determining he “fostered a hostile work environment and engaged in sexual harassment” by giving gifts and lavishing attention on two young female staffers. The bipartisan panel began investigating the second-term North Carolina congressman earlier this year, after receiving complaints about his conduct. In a report approved by Democratic and Republican committee members, they determined there “was substantial reason to believe” Edwards broke House rules by singling out the two unidentified aides for special treatment that made them uncomfortable and harmed relations with other employees. While the investigation uncovered no evidence that Edwards engaged in sexual activity with the staffers or suggested it, his behavior likely violated provisions in the House code of conduct that prohibit sexual harassment and unwanted advances. The congressman “acknowledged at least some of the behavior at issue could be viewed as inappropriate”, but “has not acknowledged or taken responsibility for the harm he caused”, the committee wrote in its report. “A member of Congress should not single out a staffer and isolate them from other staff, make frequent comments regarding that person’s appearance and weight, send messages in the middle of the night, text staff deeply personal and seemingly romantic thoughts, intrude on personal occasions without invitation, pay for personal vacations, and spend thousands of dollars on gifts for staffers,” they continued. Edwards’s re-election campaign criticized the report, arguing its findings “completely exonerate” the congressman while saying ethics committee staff “have taken it upon themselves to write their own rules based upon an interpretation that is inconsistent with the written rule of law or House rules”. “Representative Edwards looks forward to having his name cleared and will work to ensure that the full light of day is brought on this process and that every member of Congress and the public can see the attempt to harm the congressman who has brought no harm to others,” the campaign said in a statement. If the House agrees to censure Edwards, he would have to stand in the well of the chamber while the text of a resolution rebuking him is read aloud. The congressman was already viewed as vulnerable to losing re-election to his western North Carolina district in the November midterm elections. Last week election forecaster Sabato’s Crystal Ball announced it was rating his race a “toss-up” in a sign of improving Democratic chances. “My heart goes out to the young women who took these roles to serve our community,” his Democratic opponent, Jamie Ager, said following the report’s release. “We deserve leaders with the moral character western North Carolina can be proud of.” Elected in 2022 after ousting the scandal-plagued Madison Cawthorn in the Republican primary, Edwards, a former state senator, left most of the hiring for his new office up to his chief of staff, but insisted on bringing “three young women” into his operation, according to the report. This group included a woman who was still in college and identified by the committee as “Staffer 1” and a second in her early 20s, identified as “Staffer 2”. “Both young women were subject to increasingly unusual attention from the congressman while they worked for him, creating an environment where both they and their coworkers felt uncomfortable,” the committee found. These behaviors included Edwards bringing Staffer 1 to a White House event without telling the rest of his staff, buying her flowers and texting her in advance that he was “so excited about tonight” and wanted it to be “perfect”. After the event, the staffer said Edwards tried to “pressure” her into continuing the night together, which the congressman told the committee he did not recall. He invited both staffers to private dinners, and at one point told Staffer 2 to ensure the event was not put on his calendar by his office scheduler. He would also send both “personal texts” later in the evening about planning events together or expressing “personal sentiments”, the committee found. Edwards also planned lengthy and elaborate trips with the two staffers either together or individually, at one point suggesting to Staffer 2 that they “go to Annapolis for lunch, meditate by its water, stroll about town, find a day spa, see a movie, or wipe out the casino”. “I’m probably over thinking being impulsive but I really want you to enjoy our time together nearly as much as [I] know [I] will,” he wrote in a text message to the staffer released by the committee. His actions made the two staff members uncomfortable, and when a senior employee of his office spoke to Edwards on their behalf, that staffer told the committee the congressman “got very angry” and said she “didn’t understand the unique relationship” he had with the two women. Both staffers later resigned because of his behavior, but gave Edwards other reasons why when they departed. The behavior affected the morale of his office, the committee found, with one senior aide telling investigators Edwards “lashes out at everyone on the team except” the two women. The congressman denied yelling at his staff. Another staffer said they had told Edwards that an “unfair standard existed” in his office, which he said was caused by employees being “jealous”. Even after she left his employment, Staffer 2 agreed to a trip to Las Vegas with Edwards, saying she felt pressured to do so in part because he had influence over her being hired for another job in civil service. He paid for her flights, accommodation at the Bellagio hotel and a show at the Sphere. After receiving a bouquet of flowers upon arrival, Staffer 2 texted Edwards: “I’m almost ready and just got the flowers – they’re very pretty. Thank you! I did want to flag that the message made me uncomfortable. Just want to make sure this trip isn’t meant to be anything it’s not?” “Understood, and agree. I’m sorry it made you uncomfortable. Nothing was meant by it, other than what was intended to be a cute play on the name of the arrangement,” Edwards responded. Photograph: Helena Karlsson/NWT View image in fullscreen Joyce Thomas, 78, is now taking the case to a higher court. Photograph: Helena Karlsson/NWT Sweden British widow, 78, told to leave Sweden under Brexit rules after living there for 21 years Authorities say application to stay was made too late, as UK officials say Sweden takes ‘stricter approach’ than other EU countries Lisa O’Carroll Mon 10 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 08.16 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A 78-year-old British widow who has lived in Sweden for 21 years is fighting deportation from the country after authorities told her a post-Brexit application to stay had been submitted too late. Her case is the latest of 2,500 British people ordered to leave the country after Brexit in what campaigners and the UK’s Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) have said is an inexplicably hardline approach taken by the Swedish authorities. It comes two years after Sweden threatened to deport a British woman with dementia in a care home shortly before she died. Joyce Thomas, a retired nurse, was given just four weeks to leave Sweden in November, three years after her husband had died, causing huge distress. After being widowed, Thomas downsized with her dog to an apartment in Hammarö, which is close to her son and grandchildren, and to her husband’s grave. She said she sometimes felt overwhelmed by the distress of what was happening. “It is unbelievable at my age to be chucked out after being in a country for so long, when you’ve done absolutely nothing wrong,” Thomas said. “I have no criminal record, no driving penalties, nothing. And I have lived here on my own financial means. I just think nobody has actually looked into this thing. I mean, if it was their family or mother, they wouldn’t like them to be in this situation.” Holding back tears, she said: “I am not young, and the idea I would have to come back and forth to visit my son and grandchildren and to visit my husband’s grave here … it is just horrible when you sit and digest it all.” View image in fullscreen Joyce Thomas and her late husband, Gwynne. Photograph: Joyce Thomas Her husband, Gwynne, died in 2023 of cancer. It was on a trip back from the UK in 2022, when they visited their second son in Brighton, that they first learned they should have made a formal application to stay in Sweden after Brexit. She said her husband had been meticulous at keeping up with news relevant to British people in Sweden and had taken responsibility for all the administration in their household. She was sure he would have made the Brexit application had he known about it. While late applications are permissible under the UK’s withdrawal agreement with the EU, Thomas’s submission was rejected in 2024 as she could not demonstrate “reasonable grounds” for applying late. A subsequent application to stay under national immigration laws was also rejected. With the help of lawyers who are working pro bono, she is now taking the case to a higher court. “When Gwynne died it was the worst thing. We were married for 55 years; he was my best friend and meant everything to me after all those years. But, you know, it [his death] was an end. This is just unbearable limbo. It is horrible. I am not young. I have already moved from a house to a flat – and to start moving again and looking for another place? I will be dead by the time I would be settled.” The former business secretary Peter Kyle, who is MP for Hove and Portslade, said the case was “deeply concerning”. View image in fullscreen Sweden also tried to deport Kathleen Poole, seen here in a dementia care home with her son Wayne and daughter-in-law Angelica. Photograph: Angelica Poole He told the Guardian: “While immigration decisions in Sweden are a matter for the Swedish authorities, I have consistently believed that the rights of UK nationals who exercised free movement rights before Brexit should be treated fairly and with compassion.” He urged Sweden to review her case. “I hope the authorities will carefully consider all the circumstances of Mrs Thomas’s case, including her long residence in Sweden, her family connections, and the humanitarian factors involved.” The FCDO has also expressed concern, not just about Thomas but about the wider hardline approach taken by Sweden to British people living in the country since before Brexit. Data shows that Sweden has the highest number of Brexit-related deportations of Britons of all EU member states. According to Eurostat data, 2,500 British nationals have been ordered to leave the country since Brexit, one-third of the entire number of removal orders issued across the 27-member bloc since Brexit in 2021. An FCDO spokesperson said: “We regularly raise concerns regarding Sweden’s protection of citizens’ rights with both the Swedish authorities and the European Commission, which is responsible for monitoring the implementation and application of citizens’ rights matters in EU member states.” Article 18 of the EU-UK withdrawal agreement allows for late applications on “reasonable grounds”. But UK government sources said they believed Sweden was “taking a considerably stricter approach” than others. The result is that “in practice individuals are not likely to have their reasonable grounds accepted”. According to the most recent European Commission annual report on implementation of the WA, almost 4,000 applicants for post-Brexit residency status in Sweden were refused, out of 14,200 made. By contrast, Bulgaria, which has a similar number of applicants at around 16,000, refused just five people, and Belgium, which had 13,000 applicants, refused 605, according to the same report. According to FCDO analysis, Sweden’s refusal rate of 27.5% is three times higher than any other member state and considerably higher than the EU average of between 3% and 4%. View image in fullscreen Joyce Thomas, 78, in her garden in August, She is facing removal from Sweden over hardline Brexit policy. Photograph: Felix Andler A spokesperson for the Swedish immigration authority, Migrationsverket, said: “In exceptional circumstances, it is still possible to submit a late application. The applicant must explain in writing why they were unable to apply within the prescribed period. Simply stating that the person was unaware of the requirement to apply is not, in itself, considered a sufficient explanation.” The withdrawal agreement also calls for “proportionality” in any decisions to remove residency rights. “We think the proportionality is really hard to see here: that somebody’s life can be upended, simply because they missed a deadline to fill out a form that with no information communicated at all to them,” said Felix Andler, a doctor and friend of the Thomas family who is supporting her. This article was amended on 10 August 2026 because an earlier version said that Peter Kyle is the MP “for Brighton”. In fact he represents the constituency of Hove and Portslade. https://www.dw.com/en/greece-migrants-cl.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JHsg Greece has toughened up on asylum-seekers [Photo: 2021, Samos] Image: Nicolas Economou/NurPhoto/picture alliance Advertisement Migrants clashed with police at a detention center in northern Greece, with 35 having escaped the premises after cutting through a perimeter fence before police detained about half of them again, authorities said on Sunday. Greece is a major point of entry for migrants to Europe , and the country's conservative prime minister has introduced tough rules to deport those who've been denied asylum in the country. Greece, along with other European Union countries, for example, is in talks with African countries about establishing centers for failed asylum-seekers, a move that has drawn criticism from international rights groups. Crete fears more migrant arrivals could hurt tourism To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Police deploy flashbangs during clashes Police said they called for reinforcement to the detention center in Sintiki, a few kilometers from the Bulgarian border, after migrants threw rocks at police. Authorities used flash-bang grenades against people during those clashes, which they said lasted until the early hours of Sunday morning. At least five migrants were injured and taken to the hospital. Police recaptured 17 of those who escaped and the search continued for 18 others. The temporary accommodation center houses about 450 people while their applications are processed, a protracted procedure that can take a long time. https://www.firstcomicsnews.com/dont-mis.text: News The international celebration of the ultimate lawman of the future, Judge Dredd! Taking place on Saturday 3 October , The Day of Dredd is a titanic celebration of one of the most famous characters in comics history, with special signings across the UK and abroad — plus extra special swag for lucky Dredd-ites! John Wagner, Mick McMahon, Barry Kitson, Colin MacNeil and John Higgins head up the list of top creators who will be signing at Forbidden Planet stores in Birmingham, Bristol, Cambridge, Camden, Liverpool and London, Forbidden Planet International stores in Belfast, Glasgow, Manchester, Norwich and Sheffield, Books With Pictures in Portland, Oregon – and the first ever official 2000 AD signing at Knihkupectví KRAKATIT in Prague, Czechia! And early bird fans will find that participating stores will have special limited edition stickers and bookmarks available! Don’t miss the chance to dive into some Dredd on 3 October — obey the Day of Dredd! Signings will run 2pm – 3pm unless otherwise indicated: Forbidden Planet Birmingham: D’Israeli, Dave Kendall, Ian Edginton, INJ Culbard, Mike Perkins, Pye Parr Forbidden Planet Bristol: Anthony Williams, Dylan Teague, Lee Carter, Patrick Goddard Forbidden Planet Cambridge: Steven Austin Forbidden Planet Camden: Rob Williams, Liam Sharp (runs 12.30pm – 1.30pm ) Forbidden Planet Liverpool: Joe Currie, John Higgins, Leigh Gallagher, Sally Jane Hurst Forbidden Planet London: Ben Willsher, Boo Cook, Chris Weston, Dan Cornwell, John Wagner, Laura Bailey, Silvia Califano, Simon Davis (runs until 3.30pm ) Forbidden Planet Southampton: Mick McMahon Forbidden Planet International Belfast: PJ Holden Forbidden Planet International Glasgow: Colin MacNeil, Tom Foster Forbidden Planet International Manchester: Andy Diggle, Robbie Morrison Forbidden Planet International Norwich: Barry Kitson, Jake Lynch Forbidden Planet International Sheffield: Nick Percival, Staz Johnson, Peter Doherty Knihkupectví KRAKATIT, Prague: Stewart K Moore (runs 10am – 3pm ) Books With Pictures, Portland OR: Arthur Wyatt (runs from 1pm ) The Day of Dredd is the perfect day for readers new and old to discover 2000 AD ’s biggest character and Britain’s greatest comics export — a hardline future cop created by John Wagner ( A History of Violence ) and Carlos Ezquerra ( Preacher ), who has been bringing justice to the mean streets of the vast Mega-City One for almost half a century, both thrilling readers and satirising everything from Margaret Thatcher to Donald Trump, from fad fashions to freedom fighters. As well as helping launch the careers of some of comics’ biggest names, Dredd has become one of the most iconic characters in British comics and even part of the English language! Other book and comic book stores supporting The Day of Dredd include: The Darl Knight in Darlington , UK Lighthouse Comics in Folkestone , UK Dave’s Comics in Brighton , UK OK Comics in Leeds , UK Beccles Books in Beccles, Suffolk , UK Books & Bevs in York , UK Ink & Ember in Peterborough and Stamford, UK Books With Pictures in Portland and Eugene, Oregon, USA Plot Twist Comics and Games in Springfield, Missouri , USA Warlockcomics in Los Angeles, California , USA Rosie’s Comics in Amherst, Virginia , USA 717 Comics in Georgetown, Texas , USA Zeppelin Comics in Benicia, California , USA Funky Town Comics in Dayton, Ohio , USA With the 50 th anniversary of 2000 AD and Judge Dredd fast approaching in February 2027, with special plans to celebrate the occasion to be announced in the coming months, The Day of Dredd is a chance for fans to pass on their passion for The Law as well as for new readers looking for a way into one of the most important characters in comics. In addition to the long-running and best-selling Judge Dredd: The Complete Case Files series, the Essential Judge Dredd line of graphic novel collections gives readers the opportunity to encounter the big epic storylines that have influenced not just comics over the last fifty years but global culture!
